text: Imagine an agent that handles customer follow-up. You might happily let that agent find a relevant account information, draft the response, maybe even update an internal status field. But would you really trust that agent to change the customer's commercial terms or send a final message without you? Probably not, right? That difference matters because you don't give an agent autonomy all at once. You decide how much authority it has for each part of the work. Now we define authority as a dial with five positions. It suggests the agent recommends what should happen, but you remain responsible for doing it. At prepare, it creates the draft, proposes an update, or suggests a next action. At act with approval, it can execute the action, but pauses first for your decision. At act within bounds, it can execute without asking when clearly defined conditions are met. And at run and escalate, it can carry the workflow forward itself, only involving you when something falls outside of its boundaries. These are not maturity levels that every agent should climb. The right setting really depends on the action being taken. Now one useful question to set that dial is what happens if this action is wrong? If the mistake is easy to notice and easy to reverse, you can usually allow more independence. But if it affects a customer, money, sensitive information, compliance, or an important commitment, you want tighter control. There always needs to be a boundary between agents that assist and agents that execute changes in real systems. Once AI can create side effects, human control becomes way more important. And there is another factor which is uncertainty. When the situation is ambiguous, the agent should know that asking is a part of doing the job well. And this means that the same workflow can have several positions on the dial. An agent could independently retrieve information, prepare a recommendation, update a low risk internal field, request approval before contacting a customer and escalate when information conflicts. That is often way better than putting an approval step everywhere. Because too many routine approvals create friction and can make it so that people pay less attention to the decisions that actually matter. So when you design an agentic workflow, don't ask how autonomous should this agent be, but ask for each action what is the lowest level of human control that still keeps the consequences acceptable. And that is the real autonomy dial.
